scenario: Today's infrastructure track asks how to spend compute on what actually limits throughput or tail latency, without breaking quality or time limits. Ads ranking pushes quantization to 6 bits while still holding a very tight error bar. Collectives try to stop occupying compute units, and a compiler puts GPU-initiated communication and computation into the same intermediate representation. Storage movement picks the path with a better tail per phase, decode scheduling leaves headroom from the iteration tail, and requests whose cache has been invalidated speculate first with stale KV. On the training side, one system temporarily turns idle rollout GPUs into trainers while the long tail finishes, and another shrinks the trainable fine-tuning state to scalars on fixed directions. Edge quantization and an Ascend kernel-optimization benchmark turn the upkeep of formats, and whether existing implementations can still be made faster, into questions one can measure.

papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.authors: Yavuz Yetim, Bor-Yiing Su, Zhe Wang, Arthur Liu, Pranav Sharma, Ying Wang, Randy Shuai, Luke Pfister, Ruichao Xiao, Bill Zhao, Zihao Liu, Liyuan Li, Jiangyuan Li, Gaoxiang Liu, Nathan Yan, Geonhwa Jeong, Jatin Chhugani, Elias Ellison, Uladzimir Pashkevich
papers.abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model
papers.summary: Ads ranking models are extremely sensitive to quantization error. A launch bar often requires that normalized entropy stay within 0.01% of the baseline, much tighter than the accuracy loss large language models often tolerate, so lower-bit formats have been hard to put into production. The authors try microscaling 8-bit and 6-bit formats on two production ads ranking models on the AMD MI350X, and enable 6-bit compute only on layers that still pass the bar. Relative to the existing FP8 configuration, selective 6-bit use raises end-to-end throughput of Model B by 7.6% to 14.3%, and every evaluated prediction task remains inside the launch bar. The end-to-end gain shrinks as the batch grows, and the current activation layout still does not carry the full kernel speedup into whole-model throughput. ==If an ads ranker cannot clear the quality bar, a faster low-bit kernel is of no use==. For teams that want lower precision to raise throughput in recommendation and advertising, the point is to choose a format per layer, rather than compressing the whole model to a lower bit width at once.

papers.title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Mathew Jacob, Morgan Borjigin-Wang, Kan Zhu, Po Hao Chen, Yi Pan, Andy Ruan, Nayani Modugula, Ethan Lavi, Luis Ceze, Malte Schwarzkopf, Akshay Narayan, Deepti Raghavan, Stephanie Wang
papers.abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-p
papers.summary: In synchronous, colocated reinforcement learning, inference engines often sit idle waiting for a few very long generations, or decode inefficiently at very small batch sizes, and GPUs go underused. While the long tail is still running, the authors temporarily repurpose some rollout GPUs for training, and migrate unfinished generations among inference engines to raise decode throughput, while keeping on-policy training semantics. An adaptive policy chooses when to migrate, so each task and hardware setup does not need a hand-tuned schedule. On H200, end-to-end speedup over the colocated baseline reaches 1.36 times, and the system recovers up to about 97% of utilization-optimal throughput. ==To speed up on-policy training, first reuse the compute that sits idle while waiting for the long tail==. For teams training large language models with reinforcement learning, this reclaims wasted GPU time in a colocated setup without switching to off-policy training.

papers.title: Zero-SM NCCL: A Systematic Guide to Designing and Deploying SM-Free GPU Communication
papers.authors: Zhenhao He, Siyuan Shen, Ke Wen, Prajwal Singhania, Shiqing Fan, Youngeun Kwon, Sangkug Lym, Vasudevan Rengasamy, Vishnuswaroop Ramesh, Yicheng Qiang, Craig Belusar, Jeff Hammond, Torsten Hoefler
papers.abstract: GPU communication libraries such as NCCL use Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) for data movement and synchronization, slowing overlapped computation at a cost that grows with interconnect bandwidth. We present Zero-SM NCCL, which communicates within and across scale-up domains without launching any SM kernel. It synchronizes through CUDA stream memory operations, moves data asynchronously with copy engines within a scale-up domain, and drives network RDMA from a stream-ordered CPU proxy. It supports data-movement collectives such as AllGather and AlltoAll, plus one-sided ncclPutSignal and ncclWaitSignal APIs. On GB200 NVL72 and B200 NVL8 systems, Zero-SM collectives reach up to 1.36x higher AllGather bandwidth than NCCL's legacy SM-based kernels and cut the median slowdown of overlapped GEMMs from 33% to 4%, at a higher latency per operation. In Megatron-LM training, they accelerate FSDP by up to 3.5%, and one-sided puts accelerate pipeline parallelism by up to 15%. Zero-SM communication
papers.summary: GPU communication libraries often use compute units to move data and synchronize, and the cost of stealing compute grows as interconnect bandwidth rises. The authors instead complete collectives with copy engines and network transfers driven by a CPU proxy, without launching a compute kernel for communication. On newer high-bandwidth systems, the median slowdown of overlapped matrix multiplications falls from about 33% to 3.9%, and AllGather bandwidth rises by up to 1.36 times, though latency per operation is higher. Training runs have seen speedups in fully sharded data parallelism and in pipeline parallelism, but the authors stress this is not a win everywhere. ==Not every transfer is worth taking off the compute units==. Large transfers in compute-bound jobs, and deep pipelines with large bubbles, tend to pay off, while small messages and host-bound workloads can lose. For teams overlapping communication in a training framework, whether to turn off compute-unit communication should depend on message size and where the bottleneck sits.

papers.title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
papers.authors: Javid Baydamirli, Ismayil Ismayilov, Kaan Oktay, Didem Unat
papers.abstract: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.
papers.summary: Machine learning systems often specialize computation to the workload and the hardware, but communication still lives in generic libraries, whose device code and transport choices a high-level compiler cannot see. The authors put GPU-initiated communication into a kernel's intermediate representation, plan completions, synchronization, and batching together with computation, and lower the result to specialized transport code. Completions are planned around buffer lifetimes, and memory ordering is optimized across different GPUs. On H100 GPUs, small messages can be sent 3.3 times faster than with NVSHMEM. When vLLM serves a very large mixture-of-experts model, responses are up to 1.29 times faster than with a specialized expert-parallel communication library, and memory and register use are smaller as well. ==Only when communication joins the same compilation pipeline as compute can the transport be specialized to the task==. For teams running large-scale training and inference communication, this is closer to the specialization already common on the compute side than tuning a generic communication library alone.

papers.title: User-Schedulable Approximations for Quantized Tensor Programs
papers.abstract: Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law
papers.summary: When language models are quantized to run on edge devices, every weight format must be paired with every activation format and instruction set, so the number of kernels a library must maintain grows quickly. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, only 8 of 54 weight-activation pairs on the authors' Arm CPU test have an optimized tiled matrix multiplication, and the rest compute one block dot product at a time. The authors also put value approximations into the compiler: they specify an algorithm, choose how values are encoded and decoded, and schedule the resulting computations, generating hundreds of kernels from one matrix-product algorithm and one schedule library. The application uses about 3.7 times less code than GGML and KleidiAI. ==A format should not be hard-wired into a handwritten kernel; it can be a program the compiler can schedule==. For teams that must maintain many quantized kernels on the edge, encoding, decoding, and computation can share one scheduling path, rather than handwriting a kernel for every format.

papers.title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
papers.authors: Ziqing Wen, Xiaohui Song, Jiahuan Wang, Ping Luo, Junlin Zeng, Dongsheng Li, Kele Xu, Tao Sun
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Q
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning aims to change fewer parameters without losing quality, but existing methods still often leave a large trainable state, and optimizer states occupy memory as well. The authors learn only a set of scalar coefficients per layer: the input basis is fixed from task activations, the output dictionary is assigned at random, computation first aggregates output atoms before applying them to tokens, and compatible layers can share a dictionary. On commonsense reasoning, this reaches accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of LoRA's trainable parameters. On Qwen2.5-7B, peak training memory is 20% lower than LoRA and throughput is 6% higher, and the method remains competitive on mathematical and code-generation tasks. ==The trainable state need not be a full low-rank matrix; learning scalars on fixed directions can be enough==. For memory-tight fine-tuning, this puts adaptation quality, the size of the trainable state, and training efficiency together, rather than comparing final scores alone.

papers.title: TailGuard-GDS: Tail-Safe Control of GPU Storage Data Movement
papers.authors: Jiaqi Liu, Fan Yang, Xiaohang Shi, Xianzhe Zhang, Tao Jiang, Guojun Yuan, Zhan Wang, Guangming Tan
papers.abstract: AI runtimes move state between NVMe storage and GPU memory on critical paths. GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes host staging, yet our eight-H100 measurements show it is not consistently tail-optimal for semantically identical GPU-buffer operations. The preferred path varies with operation, request size, concurrency, placement, and resource contention; bandwidth and tail-latency winners can disagree. Frameworks specify what moves and when, while GPU I/O stacks expose mechanisms; neither combines phase semantics with measured tail behavior to choose a delivery plan. We present TailGuard-GDS, a runtime that selects a semantically equivalent plan per application phase. It profiles plans varying backend, request shape, and placement, minimizes GPU-visible tail latency under phase constraints, and revisits decisions as conditions change. Resource reuse keeps policy lookup and switching at microsecond-scale overhead. Integrated with PyTorch FSDP and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, TailGuard reduces FSDP step
papers.summary: When a training or inference system moves state between NVMe and GPU memory on the critical path, a direct storage path is not always best for tail latency. Which path is faster changes with the operation, request size, concurrency, and contention, and the winner for bandwidth can disagree with the winner for tail latency. The authors pick a semantically equivalent delivery plan per application phase, decide from measured tail latency, and revisit the choice when conditions change. Integrated with PyTorch FSDP, this cuts step p95 by 18.4% and GPU-idle p95 by 25.3% versus the strongest fixed path. Across several eight-GPU ZeRO workloads, step tail latency also falls relative to always staging through the host or always using a direct path. ==Data movement should not be judged by average bandwidth alone; what matters is the tail latency a phase actually fears==. For large-model training that pages state in and out of storage, always using a direct path or always staging through the host can worsen the tail in some phases.

papers.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
papers.authors: Ishaan Datta, Alind Khare, Koushik Kumar Dey, Ratnesh Jamidar, Anand Kumar Singh
papers.abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent ov
papers.summary: Interactive language model services must bound both time to the first token and the gap between later tokens. A decode jitter delays every request in the current batch, and a long reply spans many steps, so even rare overruns cause many service-level misses. Schedulers that already watch those targets often fill each step's prefill budget until the predicted latency just meets the gap target, leaving no room when the prediction is off or the host stalls. The authors calibrate how much prefill each step can carry from the measured tail of its own iteration latency, leave headroom, and serve the shortest waiting prompt first. In aggregated serving, SLO goodput reaches 2.4 to 2.9 times that of the strongest baseline. With prefill and decode disaggregated, many more requests also meet the objective. ==To keep decoding steady, a step must not schedule prefill right up to the line==. For inference services that must keep a streaming gap, leaving headroom from the tail is closer to the real experience than only pushing down the average gap.

papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
papers.summary: Agent sessions often edit the context, which invalidates cached KV state, so a request must wait to prefill again before it can decode, and latency grows. In a disaggregated serving system, the authors use the invalidated KV to draft speculative tokens, then verify those drafts against the exact KV after prefill and commit only what passes. Speculation is scheduled when decode resources are underused, and it yields when drafts are unlikely to be accepted, so those resources can still serve more promising requests first. On a two-GPU testbed with coding-agent sessions across three model families, all-request speedup over vLLM is 1.05 to 1.19 times at moderate load. Cluster-level simulations driven by real traces also show that the gains can extend to larger deployments. ==Invalidated cache need not only be thrown away and recomputed; it can be used to speculate first==. For agent services whose context is edited often, a cache miss need not wait out prefill with nothing else to do.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.authors: AI Training Platform Team, Bingwei Zhang, Jing Li, Amir Abdullin, Sihang Chen, Xin Chen, Liangjun Feng, Yingmeng Gao, Tao Guo, Junjie Huang, Dongfang Li, Zhanglian Lin, Jiajun Liu, Zekun Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Xiaodong Luo, Jian Meng, Ivan Nosov, Linyuan Qiu, Weijian Sun, Wanrui Yan, Binfan Zheng, Zhicheng Zhou, Baotian Hu, Min Zhang, Haizhou Li, Zhiquan Luo
papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels
papers.summary: Kernel benchmarks on Ascend often ask whether an agent can write an implementation from scratch, and less often whether an existing implementation can be made faster on input shapes taken from real training and inference. The authors build an optimization benchmark from real workloads, split kernels from large-model training and inference into three difficulty batches, and this report evaluates the more basic batch. About 70% of model-harness combinations have a geometric-mean speedup below 1.2 times. The same model with a different harness can still move from 1.05 times to 1.69 times even when every task is solved correctly. They also score speedup together with the tokens spent in the search, to measure how much was gained inside a budget. ==Final speedup alone shows neither how much the search cost nor whether the process was sound==. For teams training and serving on Ascend, optimization becomes a question of how much can still be squeezed under a budget, with results that must pass a correctness check, not only of writing a correct kernel.
